claims.text: Retaining a random, single-phase atomic distribution with minimal chemical short-range order is key to high-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Random atomic mixing maximizes configurational entropy.
Higher configurational entropy suppresses atomic mobility and diffusion pathways that cause phase segregation and oxidation.
Modest chemical short-range order lowers local entropy.
Chemical short-range order creates preferential sites for diffusion-driven degradation.
The as-synthesized high-entropy nanoalloys have a uniformly random atomic distribution and a single-phase structure.
High-temperature thermal annealing can produce varying degrees of chemical short-range order in the nanoalloys.
The degree of chemical short-range order modulates atomic diffusion.
The degree of chemical short-range order modulates phase-interface energies.
A fully random arrangement reduces the thermodynamic driving force for nucleation of secondary phases.
Short-range order creates favorable sites for atomic diffusion and segregation.
Short-range order initiates phase separation or oxidation at high temperature.
Nanoalloys retaining minimal short-range order will have greater phase stability than short-range-ordered samples.
Nanoalloys retaining minimal short-range order will undergo less grain growth than short-range-ordered samples.
Nanoalloys retaining minimal short-range order will have lower oxidation rates than short-range-ordered samples.
The prediction applies primarily to nanoalloys with grain sizes below approximately 100 nm.
The prediction is most relevant at 800–1000 °C under inert or controlled environments.
The effects may differ in coarse-grained or multiphase materials.
